name: Swarga Brahma Temple, Alampur
period: Early Chalukya, late 7th century; raised in honour of a Chalukya queen
summary: The most richly carved of Alampur's Navabrahma temples, Swarga Brahma was raised in honour of a Chalukya queen, and its walls still show Shiva as cosmic dancer, as destroyer of the three cities and as the endless pillar of fire.

sections.history: Swarga Brahma is among the best preserved of the nine Navabrahma temples and the one whose founding is most clearly recorded. An inscription engraved above one of its door-guardian figures states that it was built by Lokaditya Ela Arasa in honour of the queen of the Chalukya king Vinayaditya, who ruled from Badami between 681 and 696; Lokaditya is described in different accounts as a prince of the royal house or as a local feudatory. The temple therefore belongs to the last decades of the seventh century, with its consecration sometimes placed around the turn of the eighth. Like its neighbours it suffered in later raids and many of its figures were defaced, yet it remains the fullest expression of Chalukyan sculpture at Alampur.
sections.architecture: Facing east, the temple opens through a porch of six pillars ornamented with amalaka discs, with a Nandi on a raised platform before it. Within, a pillared hall leads to the sanctum, which is wrapped by a passage for circumambulation, and above it rises a curving northern tower that survives largely intact. The outer walls are the temple's glory: pilastered niches — four along each side wall, two at each end — frame Shiva as Nataraja, as Tripurantaka, as Lingodbhava, as Gangadhara and as the wandering mendicant Bhikshatana, together with Vamana, Vishnu's dwarf avatar, and the guardian gods of the directions. Ganga and Yamuna flank the sanctum doorway.
sections.legends: The name Swarga Brahma, 'Brahma of heaven', belongs to the Alampur tradition that Brahma did penance here and worshipped Shiva in nine forms. The temple's walls are themselves a book of Shaiva legend: Lingodbhava recalls the night when Brahma and Vishnu searched in vain for the ends of a boundless column of fire, Tripurantaka shows Shiva destroying the three flying cities of the demons with a single arrow, and Gangadhara receives the descending Ganga in his matted locks. That this whole cycle was offered in memory of a queen gives the temple a quiet, personal tenderness.
sections.festivals: Swarga Brahma is a protected monument and keeps no festival of its own, though the precinct around it fills at Maha Shivaratri, when pilgrims throng the Bala Brahma temple, and at Navaratri and Dasara for the goddess Jogulamba. Winter mornings, with clear low light on the carved walls, are the best time to see it. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Walk round Swarga Brahma clockwise and take the niches one by one: the dancing Shiva and the Tripurantaka panel reward close looking even where faces have been damaged. Then step back to take in the whole tower, one of the finest at Alampur. The temple stands just behind Bala Brahma, with Padma Brahma beyond it, so the three are naturally seen together.

visit.timings: Open in daylight hours as an Archaeological Survey of India monument within the Navabrahma precinct; it is not a place of daily worship. Confirm current hours and any ticketing locally.
visit.dressCode: No strict dress code applies at the monument, but modest dress is appropriate in this sacred precinct, and footwear is removed at the active shrines nearby.
visit.photography: Photography of the exterior and its sculpture is generally permitted; tripods or professional equipment may need permission from the Archaeological Survey of India. Follow the posted rules.
visit.gettingThere: Alampur is in Jogulamba Gadwal district, about 25 km from Kurnool and some 220 km south of Hyderabad, just off the Hyderabad–Bengaluru highway (NH 44). Alampur Road railway station, on the Hyderabad–Kurnool line, is about 9 km away. The temple stands behind the Bala Brahma temple, a few minutes' walk from the Jogulamba temple.
